rule: mixed: the rule line is never parsed, but splitting it into two separate sentences is what causes the trouble below — each one parses as a law that every spring tide falls at that phase, so together they say each tide falls at both. One sentence carrying the alternation keeps the rule's "and" meaning without asserting two exceptionless laws: "Spring tides occur at new moon or at full moon."
texts: bad: this is recorded as an exceptionless, definitional law — every spring tide falls at new moon — which is stronger than the sentence says and, standing beside the full-moon sentence, makes each tide fall at both phases. Combine the two phases into one sentence: "Spring tides occur at new moon or at full moon."

bad: same problem as the new-moon sentence — it is recorded as an exceptionless law that every spring tide falls at full moon, which conflicts with the new-moon sentence once both are in the knowledge base. Write the alternation once instead of as two separate laws: "Spring tides occur at new moon or at full moon."
good. every piece lands — the Keepers as a named group, the salt-bloom harvest as the thing being timed, and "to the new-moon spring tide" kept on the preposition actually used.
